newsitem.title: UK: Blair issues ministerial code as share row flares.
newsitem.headline: Blair issues ministerial code as share row flares.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair, facing a row over valuable shares held by one of his ministers, on Thursday told his government to observe a new code to prevent their personal interests conflicting with their government jobs.

But his Conservative opponents claimed the publication by Blair of a new "Ministerial Code" was a smokescreen to divert attention from the case of Lord David Simon, former chairman of British Petroleum.
Simon, appointed Minister for Trade and Competitiveness in Europe by Blair, has retained at least 247,091 shares worth two million pounds ($3.25 million) in the oil giant.

The Conservatives, who faced a series of allegations of sleaze among ministers which contributed to their defeat at the May 1 election, have latched onto the Simon affair as the first controversy over ministerial conduct in the Blair government.
Following up attacks on Simon by Conservative leader William Hague, the opposition's industry spokesman John Redwood told journalists on Thursday: "He should either resign or sell his shares."

Redwood said BP had published its profit figures for the first quarter of 1997 on May 7, the day Simon took office. Simon had a perfect opportunity to sell the shares on that day, ensuring he could face his new job without accusations of bias or profiting from "insider" knowledge, he said.

But Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett accused the Conservatives of mounting a "vindictive campaign" against a man who had given up a highly-paid job at BP to take an unpaid government post.
"You are applying...a totally different standard to David Simon from those which applied to previous Conservative ministers," she wrote in an open letter to Hague.
The government points out that Simon has undertaken not to trade in BP shares and maintains he does not deal as a minister with matters which might affect BP.
But the Conservatives say the company's interests are so broad that this is impossible given his remit.
The new document on ministers' conduct published by Blair updates one under the previous administration.
"Ministers must scrupulously avoid any danger of an actual or apparent conflict of interest between their ministerial position and their private financial interests," it said.
In its foreword, Blair tells his colleagues: "We are all here to serve and we must all serve honestly and in the interests of those who gave us our positions of trust."
Blair faced the first major test of his popularity among voters since the May 1 election on Thursday, the last day parliament will sit before a 2-1/2-month summer recess.
Labour is battling to win a parliamentary by-election in the traditionally Conservative seat of Uxbridge which would increase its majority in the 659-seat House of Commons to 180 seats.
Conservative Sir Michael Shersby died soon after he won the seat by only 724 votes.

History is against Labour -- a governing party has not taken a seat from the main opposition party at a by-election since 1960. Some voters are angry that Labour candidate Andy Slaughter has no links to the area.

But a MORI poll in the Times newspaper on Thursday showed Blair's honeymoon continues nationally. Labour won 57 percent support, just one point down on the post-election peak, with the Conservatives at 23 percent, also a point down.
At the May election, Labour won 43.2 percent of the national vote.
